passages.t: Search the streets for one just person
passages.happening:
‘Go up and down the streets of Jerusalem. Look now and take note; search her squares’ (verse 1). If Jeremiah can find a single person who acts justly and seeks the truth, God will forgive the city (verse 1). The people swear by the living LORD, but they swear falsely (verse 2). ‘They have made their faces harder than stone and refused to repent’ (verse 3).

Jeremiah thinks, These are only the poor, who do not know the way of the LORD (verse 4). He will go to the powerful, who surely know it. ‘But they too, with one accord, had broken the yoke and torn off the chains’ (verse 5). So the lion, the wolf and the leopard will strike them (verse 6).

‘Why should I forgive you?’ (verse 7). God fed them, and they ran to other gods and to other men's wives (verses 7 and 8). Should he not punish such a nation (verse 9)? The vineyard will be stripped, ‘but do not finish them off’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Swearing As surely as the LORD lives called God as witness that what was said was true. To use that oath while lying made God himself the guarantor of a falsehood.

The streets and squares were the public places of an ancient city, where business, gossip and court cases happened at the gates. Jeremiah goes looking in the places where justice should have been seen.

The search has a famous ancestor. Abraham once pleaded for Sodom, asking whether God would spare it for ten righteous people. Here the number falls to one, and still none is found. The first hearers would feel how far the city had fallen.

The wild animals of verse 6 were real dangers on the roads. They stand for the invader who would tear the land apart.
passages.later: Abraham asked for Sodom, ‘Suppose ten are found there?’ (Genesis 18:32). A psalm says the same of all people: ‘there is no one who does good, not even one’ (Psalm 14:3).
passages.hard:
Was there really not one just person in Jerusalem? What about Jeremiah himself?

The book itself knows faithful people: Jeremiah, his secretary Baruch, the officials who protected him (26:24), and Ebed-melech, who rescued him from the cistern (38:7-13). Many interpreters take the search as prophetic exaggeration, meant to expose the corruption of the city as a whole, as a psalm cries that no one does good. Others note that the search is among the public places and those who set the city's course: neither the poor nor the powerful, as a body, sought justice.

On any reading the chapter shows the depth of the city's corruption, not that God could find no one he loved. The chapter itself says God will not make a full end (verse 18).
passages.asks: God would have forgiven the city for one just person. Ask whether you would be found, if someone searched your street. And ask whether you have assumed that justice is someone else's job, the poor's or the powerful's.

passages.t: He will do nothing, they said
passages.happening:
The people have lied about the LORD, saying he will not do anything and no harm will come (verse 12). ‘The prophets are but wind, for the word is not in them’ (verse 13).

So God says to Jeremiah, ‘I will make My words a fire in your mouth and this people the wood it consumes’ (verse 14). He is bringing ‘an established nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know’ (verse 15). Its quivers are like open graves (verse 16). It will eat their harvest, their flocks, their vines and fig trees, and destroy the walled cities they trust (verse 17).

Yet even then, God says, he will not make a full end of them (verse 18). When they ask why God has done this, they are to hear: as they served foreign gods in their own land, so they will serve foreigners in a land not their own (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The people's words in verse 12 were the comfortable belief that God would do nothing. They dismissed the prophets as wind, a play on the word for spirit and breath.

Verse 15 describes the invader as an old nation with a language Judah could not understand. That fits Babylon, whose cities went back thousands of years and whose language, Akkadian, meant nothing to Hebrew speakers. It also echoes the curse of Deuteronomy 28, which warned of a nation from far away whose language Israel would not know.

Verse 19 is measure for measure. They served foreign gods at home, so they will serve foreigners abroad. The punishment matches the sin.
passages.later: The law had warned of ‘a nation whose language you will not understand’ (Deuteronomy 28:49). Zephaniah describes the same people, who say in their hearts, ‘The LORD will do nothing’ (Zephaniah 1:12).
passages.asks: The people said God would do nothing. Ask where you have quietly decided that God will not act, for good or for judgment. And ask what you dismiss as wind that may be God's word to you.

passages.t: The sea obeys, but this people does not
passages.happening:
‘Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes but do not see, who have ears but do not hear’ (verse 21). Do they not tremble before the God who set the sand as the boundary of the sea, a barrier it cannot cross? The waves roar but cannot pass (verse 22). ‘But these people have stubborn and rebellious hearts’ (verse 23). They never stopped to fear the LORD who gives the rains in season and keeps the weeks of harvest (verse 24). Their sins have kept those good things away (verse 25).

Among God's people are wicked men who lie in wait like bird-catchers and set traps for people (verse 26). ‘Like cages full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit’ (verse 27). They have grown fat and rich, and ‘They have not taken up the cause of the fatherless’ or defended the needy (verse 28).

‘A horrible and shocking thing has happened in the land’ (verse 30). ‘The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority. My people love it so, but what will you do in the end?’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The sea was the great picture of chaos in the ancient world, and yet it stops at a line of sand. The ocean obeys its Maker. God's own people do not.

The rains of autumn and spring were the life of the land. Baal worship claimed the storm god gave them. Verse 24 says the people never thanked the God who really sent them.

The fowlers of verses 26 and 27 were bird-catchers who used nets, snares and decoys and kept the birds in wicker cages to sell. The rich fill their houses with the profits of deceit the way a fowler fills a cage. Israel's law required special care for the fatherless, the widow and the foreigner, who had no one to protect them. These men grew fat while the fatherless had no one to plead their cause.

The last verse is the saddest. False prophets and priests ruling for themselves, ‘My people love it so’ (verse 31). The people wanted it that way.
passages.later: Jesus asked his disciples the question of verse 21: ‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’ (Mark 8:18). God says to the sea in Job, ‘You may come this far, but no farther’ (Job 38:11).
passages.asks: The people loved being told what they wanted to hear. Ask which voices you listen to because they comfort you, not because they are true. And ask whose cause, among the fatherless and the needy, you could take up.
